name: Alternating warm and cold showers

lead: Alternating warm and cold showers, also called contrast showers, switch between warm and cool water within a single shower. People fold the routine into daily appearance regimens for post-workout recovery, to feel alert and fresh-faced, and because proponents say it improves circulation.

The main published trials are in athletes and test recovery rather than looks. A netball study found no significant difference in repeated agility between contrast showers and passive rest, while a 2026 randomized trial in combat-sport athletes tested a four-week routine on recovery, stress hormone, heart rate variability and blood-vessel responses.

paras: The usual pattern is a warm phase followed by a short cold phase, repeated several times, finishing on whichever temperature the person prefers. People do it after training or in the morning, and the studies used about 10 to 14 minutes in total with roughly 38 to 40 degrees Celsius warm water and 13 to 18 degrees cold.

Sudden cold exposure can provoke a strong cardiovascular response and is a concern for people with heart conditions, who are generally advised to check with a clinician. Very hot water can dry the skin. Wikipedia notes systematic reviews of hydrotherapy found no clear curative effects and that evidence for benefits beyond placebo is not conclusive.

chain: Alternate warm and cold water after training
Aims at faster-feeling recovery and alertness
angle.text: People use the routine as part of a recovery and grooming habit. Any effect on looks is through recovery and training consistency and through the refreshed feeling afterward, not through a direct change to skin or hair.

lead: Alternating warm and cold showers, a form of contrast hydrotherapy, is a routine in which a person switches between warm and cold water during one shower. It descends from hydrotherapy traditions of Priessnitz and Sebastian Kneipp in the 19th century, and today appears in sports recovery and daily self-care routines. [1]

In appearance communities the routine is used as part of a daily regimen. Proponents link it to improved circulation, recovery after training that supports more regular lifting and physique building, and a fresher, more alert look. Research cited here concerns recovery measures in athletes, not skin or hair appearance. [1][2][3]
The main trials are small randomized studies of athletes, which compare contrast showers with passive rest or lukewarm showers on performance and recovery markers. [2][3]
infobox: 10 to 14 minutes, warm 38-40 C, cold 13-18 C

paras: Hydrotherapy, once called hydropathy or the water cure, uses water temperature and pressure for treatment and relief, and includes showers, baths and cold plunges. Vincenz Priessnitz led a popular revival at Graefenberg from around 1829, and Sebastian Kneipp favoured a gentler approach with methods that could be practiced cheaply at home. [1]

Proponents of alternating hot and cold water say it improves circulation and lymphatic drainage, and proponents of cold water immersion say it aids blood return and clearing of waste after exertion. [1] Shower-based contrast has become more common partly because full-immersion methods raise contamination concerns and need facilities. [1][2]

The routine is typically added to a grooming or training habit, after workouts or in the morning. In the recovery-to-physique chain people describe, feeling less sore and more alert makes consistent training easier, which over time supports muscle gain. Communities also cite a fresher look afterward, though published studies have not measured skin or complexion outcomes.

A randomized crossover study of 10 elite netball players compared a 14-minute contrast water therapy, a contrast shower and passive seated rest after a netball circuit, measuring repeated agility, skin and core temperature and perceptions at several time points up to 24 hours. The researchers examined contrast showers as a more accessible substitute for contrast water immersion. [2]

A 2026 randomized field trial assigned 60 combat-sport athletes to a four-week post-training routine of 10 minutes of alternating warm (38 to 40 C) and cold (13 to 15 C) water or a thermoneutral shower, measuring perceived recovery, morning salivary cortisol, resting heart rate variability and microvascular reactivity at baseline, after the intervention and after a two-week washout. [3]

Wikipedia reports that systematic reviews of randomized trials of hydrotherapy found no clear evidence of curative effects, citing methodological flaws, with an exception of experimental evidence that alternating hot and cold water may reduce swelling and injury in the acute stage. [1]

Wikipedia notes that Kneipp himself thought hydropathic practices could be too violent or too frequent and cause physical or emotional trauma. [1] Cold water causes a sharp cardiovascular response and is generally discussed with caution for people with heart conditions.
